ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia recently hosted its Third National Agroecology Conference at the Ministry of Agriculture Conference Center, focusing on the importance of ecological farming in combating climate change and food insecurity. Organized by PELUM Ethiopia alongside civil society and development partners, the conference gathered researchers, policymakers, and farming communities under the theme “Agroecology for Environmental Health, Sustainable Food Systems and Climate Resilience.” Key speakers emphasized the need to incorporate ecological principles into national agricultural policies, advocating for the scaling up of agroecological practices to restore degraded soils and protect smallholder farmers from extreme weather. The event featured an exhibition of indigenous seeds and local farming tools, showcasing farmer-led adaptation techniques. The conference concluded with awards recognizing outstanding contributions to seed conservation and sustainable farming. Stakeholders underscored the necessity of ongoing collaboration to implement the conference's recommendations effectively. This initiative reflects Ethiopia's commitment to enhancing climate resilience and food security through sustainable agricultural practices. (160 words)

The Summit provided an important platform for advancing Ethiopia–Russia relations, strengthening Africa–Russia cooperation, and exploring new avenues of partnership in strategic sectors. (See article) Minister of Foreign Affairs Gedion Timothewos held discussions with China’s Special Envoy for African Affairs, Liu Xianfa, on Wednesday (November 4), exchanging views on peace and security in Africa. Minister Gedion briefed the Special Envoy on the current peace and security situation in the Horn of Africa, while Liu reaffirmed China’s commitment to playing a constructive role in promoting peace and security across the continent. FM Gedion held talks with Chinese Ambassador to Ethiopia Chen Hai on Tuesday (November 3), discussing ways to deepen the two countries’ All-Weather Strategic Partnership, particularly in trade, investment and capacity building. Ambassador Chen Hai reaffirmed China’s support for Ethiopia’s development plans. State Minister Ambassador Hadera Abera met with a delegation of the European Union Political and Security Committee (PSC), led by its Chair, Ambassador Lene Vensild, on Thursday (November 5). The discussion focused on current developments in Ethiopia, the Government’s reform efforts, regional peace and security, and Ethiopia-EU relations. State Minister Ambassador Berhanu Tsegaye received His Majesty King Letsie III of the Kingdom of Lesotho to Addis Ababa on Monday (November 2) at Bole International Airport, for his working visit to Ethiopia. Ethiopia participated in the 9th Assembly of the International Solar Alliance in New Delhi, represented by Ambassador Nebiyu Tedla, who reaffirmed the country’s commitment to renewable energy and highlighted the importance of cooperation, investment and affordable clean technologies in advancing an inclusive energy transition. Addis Ababa was recognized with the 2026 Global Award for Sustainable Development in Cities on Saturday (October 31), highlighting the city’s progress in sustainable urban development and its ongoing transformation. Djibouti President Ismaïl Omar Guelleh of Djibouti received Somalia’s Speaker of the House of the People, Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur, on Monday (November 2), discussing ways to strengthen bilateral ties and strategic cooperation between the two countries. Africa and the African Union Africa’s Commemoration of the 40th Anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development at the African Union Headquarters, running from November 4-6. Convening under the urgent theme “From Resilience to Sustainable Prosperity,” the high-level opening session featured addresses from Ambassador Hadera Abera, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Awa Dabo, United Nations Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, and Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security. (See article) Senior officials from the African Union, the European Commission and EU Member States convened at the AU Headquarters in Addis Ababa on Wednesday (November 4) for the AU-EU Senior Officials’ Meeting, advancing the outcomes of the 7th AU-EU Summit held in Luanda in November 2025. The meeting focused on strengthening cooperation in peace and security, multilateralism, trade, economic development, climate action, food security, and digital and AI governance, with a view to translating the Joint Vision for 2030 into concrete actions. (See article) The African Union Commission and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies convened a high-level event on Tuesday (November 3) to advance durable solutions towards zero hunger in Africa, with AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf calling for collective action and sustained commitment to resilient agrifood systems and food security across the continent. AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf received King Letsie III of Lesotho on Tuesday (November 3), on the sidelines of the AU-IFRC High-Level Event on Advancing Durable Solutions Towards Zero Hunger in Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Leads Ethiopian Delegation to the 3rd Russia–Africa Summit A high-level Ethiopian delegation led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed successfully concluded its participation in the Third Russia–Africa Summit, held in Moscow, Russia, on October 28–29, 2026. The Summit provided an important platform for advancing Ethiopia–Russia relations, strengthening Africa–Russia cooperation, and exploring new avenues of partnership in strategic sectors. The Summit concluded with the adoption of the Declaration of the Third Russia–Africa Summit and a new Action Plan for the Russia–Africa Partnership Forum, setting out priorities for cooperation and continued political dialogue between the two sides. Addressing the plenary session of the Leaders’ Summit, Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the historic foundations of Ethiopia–Russia relations, noting that the friendship between the two countries spans more than a century and is rooted in mutual respect, cooperation, and solidarity. Recalling Russia’s humanitarian contribution following the Battle of Adwa in 1896, the Prime Minister noted that the Russian Red Cross Mission provided medical assistance to wounded Ethiopian soldiers and translated a medical guide into Amharic. He described this historical contribution as a meaningful example of knowledge exchange and solidarity between the two nations. The Prime Minister went on to emphasize that Ethiopia’s development priorities are anchored in three strategic pillars: food security, energy, and knowledge. He underscored the importance of strengthening agricultural productivity through cooperation in farm machinery, agro-processing, and industrial development. On energy cooperation, he highlighted Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia towards the development of the country’s first nuclear power plant, emphasizing the importance of diversifying the national energy mix, strengthening local technical expertise, and adhering to the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). He also pointed to the broader applications of nuclear science in healthcare, including cancer treatment. Regarding knowledge and technological development, the Prime Minister highlighted Ethiopia’s ambition to advance artificial intelligence capabilities through the establishment of Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa. He invited Russian universities and research institutions to collaborate with their Ethiopian counterparts in education, research, and technological innovation. He further called for stronger economic cooperation through joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceuticals and machinery, while underscoring the importance of facilitating trade and developing efficient payment channels. On regional and international affairs, Prime Minister Abiy reiterated Ethiopia’s support for African-led mediation and negotiated solutions to conflicts on the continent. He also welcomed the adoption of the new Action Plan, stressing the need to translate summit commitments into measurable results. The Prime Minister concluded by expressing Ethiopia’s readiness to host the next Russia–Africa Summit in Addis Ababa, the seat of the African Union, underscoring the country’s commitment to strengthening the partnership between Africa and Russia. As part of his engagements in Moscow, PM Abiy attended the airshow and handover ceremony marking the delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets to the Ethiopian Defense Force. In his remarks on the occasion, the Prime Minister described the delivery as an important milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its defense capabilities and safeguard national sovereignty. He stated that the acquisition was made in accordance with an earlier agreement with the Russian Government and expressed appreciation to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery ahead of the agreed schedule. The Prime Minister also indicated that Ethiopia would receive four batteries of the S-400 air defense system. He underscored that strengthening the operational readiness of the Ethiopian Defense Force is an essential component of the country’s efforts to deter aggression, safeguard its security, and contribute to regional stability. Expanding beyond strategic and military cooperation into the cultural and intellectual sphere, the visit also featured the presentation of the Russian-language edition of the Prime Minister’s foundational philosophy book, Medemer. During their bilateral discussions, Prime Minister Abiy handed over a copy of the newly translated book to President Vladimir Putin. On the sidelines of the Summit, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ambassador Hadera Abera held discussions with Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation Georgy Borisenko. Their discussions focused on strengthening the Ethiopia–Russia strategic partnership, expanding economic and energy cooperation, and enhancing collaboration on regional peace, security, and multilateral issues. Another significant outcome of the Summit was the signing of three bilateral agreements between Ethiopia and Russia. The agreements comprise an Intergovernmental Agreement on Dejazmach Balcha Hospital in Addis Ababa, a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ethiopian News Agency (ENA) and Russia’s ITAR-TASS, and another Memorandum of Understanding between ENA and Russia Today (RT). The agreement concerning Dejazmach Balcha Hospital underscores the shared commitment of the two countries to strengthening healthcare cooperation, modernizing medical infrastructure, and improving the delivery of health services. The two media cooperation agreements are expected to provide a framework for enhanced information exchange, professional collaboration, and institutional partnerships between the respective media organizations. Ethiopia Commemorates 40th Anniversary of the Right to Development with UN and AU Officials Africa’s Commemoration of the 40th Anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on the Right to Development at the African Union Headquarters, running from November 4-6. Convening under the urgent theme “From Resilience to Sustainable Prosperity,” the high-level opening session featured addresses from Ambassador Hadera Abera, State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Awa Dabo, United Nations Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, and Ambassador Bankole Adeoye, AU Commissioner for Political Affairs, Peace and Security. In his address, Ambassador Hadera Abera said the gathering was not merely a moment to mark a historical milestone, but an opportunity to reflect on four decades of achievements and to deliberate on what remains to be done to fully realize the Declaration’s objectives. He recalled the vision set out in its first article: that every human person should participate in, contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development, alongside the full realization of human rights and fundamental freedoms. The Ambassador acknowledged the progress the world has made since 1986, citing reduced extreme poverty, improved access to education and health care, longer life expectancy, and advances in science and technology. He noted, however, that the global South continues to face structural impediments, including external debt burdens and technological and financing gaps, which weigh on the development prospects of States operating in a rapidly evolving global landscape. Ambassador Hadera underscored that the Declaration affirmed a truth African visionaries had long understood: development is not a privilege, nor mere charity or aid, but a fundamental human right owed to every citizen. He pointed out that Africa had anchored this principle in the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights well before 1986, demonstrating that economic and social progress must advance together with civil liberties. Today, he said, the right continues to drive the African Union’s Agenda 2063: The Africa We Want, as well as the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Describing the theme as fitting for Ethiopia’s ongoing development trajectory, the Ambassador said Ethiopia, as a founding member of both the OAU and the UN, has consistently championed the view that true self-determination is inseparable from economic independence, food security, and self-reliant national development. Human dignity, he stressed, cannot be fully realized without freedom from poverty and access to quality healthcare, clean energy, education, and meaningful economic opportunity. He said Ethiopia’s home-grown economic reform agenda has taken historic steps toward economic resilience, environmental sustainability, and food sovereignty, translating the right to development from paper into tangible outcomes for its people. Through targeted investments in cluster farming, wheat self-sufficiency programs, and irrigation, he said, Ethiopia has moved from being a net importer to an exporter of wheat. The Ambassador also pointed to the Green Legacy Initiative, under which about 56 billion tree seedlings have been planted since 2019, restoring degraded lands, fighting climate change, and building sustainable livelihoods for rural communities. By integrating fruit-bearing and livestock fodder trees into local farming systems, he said, the initiative also advances food security. He described the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Africa’s largest hydroelectric dam, planned and financed through Ethiopian capacity, as a project that is generating electricity to connect the region and embodies a model of self-reliance and shared, sustainable growth. GERD, he said, is an answer to Ethiopians’ centuries-old quest to use their resources for their own advancement, and a remarkable transformative project in Africa’s modern development history. It stands as a testament to Ethiopia’s commitment to the right to development and a practical embodiment of the Declaration’s core principle that citizens are the owners and primary beneficiaries of development’s fruits. “These initiatives prove that when a nation invests in its people, infrastructure, and natural resources, the Right to Development becomes a living reality,” he said. Speaking candidly about the realities facing the continent, Ambassador Hadera pointed to severe systemic obstacles: an unfair global financial system, crushing debt burdens, geopolitical shocks, and the disproportionate impacts of a climate crisis Africa did not create. These structural inequities, he said, strain the continent’s ability to make progress. Even so, he insisted that Africa is not a passive recipient of circumstances. Its greatest strengths lie within its own borders: a vibrant, innovative youth population, dynamic entrepreneurs, and unmatched natural wealth. He called on African countries to unlock the power of youth, empower women, and build resilient economies that leave no one behind, aligning efforts and moving forward together. At the same time, he urged continued demands for urgent reform of the global financial architecture. Africa, he said, requires equitable access to capital, fair trade systems, and robust climate adaptation financing so that its development strategies can flourish unhindered by external systemic imbalances. Concluding his remarks, Ambassador Hadera said development rights must not remain abstract concepts; they must be felt in family homes, children’s classrooms, and young people’s everyday businesses. He called the commemoration an occasion for renewed international solidarity, stronger domestic policies, and active partnerships among governments, civil society, and the private sector, urging participants to forge bold commitments that deliver tangible, lasting progress for every African citizen. Also addressing the session, Deputy High Commissioner Awa Dabo said the story of the right to development cannot be told without Africa. Long before development was firmly established in the global human rights discourse, she noted, African leaders, jurists, and civil society were advancing its essential foundations, including self-determination, sovereignty over natural resources, equitable participation, and international solidarity. “Africa was not simply a beneficiary of the right to development,” she said. “Africa was one of its principal architects.” She pointed to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights as the legally binding expression of this vision, and said Africa’s voice today is not only relevant but indispensable. Forty years on, she warned, formidable barriers remain, among them unequal trading relationships, unsustainable debt, shrinking development finance, and persistent illicit financial flows, with consequences felt most sharply by people already facing poverty, exclusion, and discrimination. Growth achieved at any cost to people and the planet, she stressed, is not development. Describing Agenda 2063 as a powerful roadmap, the Deputy High Commissioner said the task now is implementation: integrating the right to development into national plans, public budgets, monitoring systems, and accountability frameworks. She said the conference’s proposed Addis Ababa Outcome Statement offers a chance to set concrete commitments on domestication, financing, monitoring, and accountability. She added that implementation also depends on international cooperation, noting Africa’s leadership in advancing discussion of a draft international covenant on the right to development. The right, she cautioned, must not be reduced to an adversarial North-South debate, because it is a universal human right relevant to every society and every person. In his opening statement, Ambassador Bankole Adeoye recalled that the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights entered into force six weeks before the UN adopted the Declaration in 1986. Africa, he said, did not wait for the world to proclaim this right, because through Article 22, which recognizes the right of all peoples to economic, social and cultural development, it had already made it binding treaty law. He said the theme captures both Africa’s pride and its impatience, and stressed that resilience must never become the ceiling of its ambition. Ambassador Adeoye said the African Union supports a robust, legally binding International Covenant on the Right to Development. “Declarations inspire, but obligations deliver,” he said. He underscored that Agenda 2063 and its Second Ten-Year Implementation Plan translate Article 22 into measurable outcomes, which must be domesticated in national plans, budgets, and accountability systems. He also noted that in August 2026, the Peace and Security Council requested the integration of human rights indicators into the Continental Early Warning System. On the green transition, the Commissioner said Africa will not accept one that repeats the injustices of past extraction, and called for responsible business conduct, fair financing, debt sustainability, and action against illicit financial flows. He added that artificial intelligence must be governed by equality, participation, transparency, and accountability. Concluding, he said the right to development must be fulfilled “no

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed led a high-level delegation to the Third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow, focusing on enhancing Ethiopia-Russia relations and exploring partnerships in strategic sectors. The summit concluded with a declaration and an action plan to foster cooperation. Additionally, Ethiopia commemorated the 40th anniversary of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development at the African Union, emphasizing the need for sustainable prosperity. Minister Gedion Timothewos engaged with China's Special Envoy for African Affairs to discuss peace and security, while State Minister Ambassador Hadera Abera met with the EU Political and Security Committee to address regional developments. The week underscored Ethiopia's active role in regional diplomacy and its focus on development and security partnerships.

ethiopia.title: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests
ethiopia.content: Africa: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: AU Commission Chief Urges Parties to Focus On Serving Citizens and Strengthening Nat'l Interests 6 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Political parties must go beyond seeking power and focus on serving citizens, strengthening democratic governance and building consensus on Africa's development priorities, African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf said today. Addressing the second African Political Parties Summit 2026 underway in Addis Ababa, the Chairperson highlighted the central role of political parties in advancing democratic governance, peace and development in line with the African Union Agenda 2063. Youssouf said political parties have three major responsibilities: developing social and economic policies that serve citizens, building bridges between citizens and state institutions, and raising awareness about the broader interests of their countries. "Are they meant to conquer power? Or is the mission wider than that?" he asked, stressing that political parties should serve the public and promote national interests rather than narrow political, ethnic or sectarian interests. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Chairperson also underscored the role of opposition parties in monitoring government actions and ensuring public accountability. On constitutional governance, Youssouf said states have a fundamental responsibility to protect their constitutions, organize credible elections and ensure respect for fundamental freedoms. "In case of disagreements on those critical issues, dialogue must always prevail," he noted. He further highlighted the importance of transparency in political party financing, saying strict rules are necessary to prevent corruption and external influences. Referring to the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, the Chairperson said the instrument recognizes political pluralism and promotes the rights and responsibilities of ruling and opposition parties. He also described the Maputo Protocol as an important foundation for women's participation in political life, emphasizing the need for forums bringing together women and young people to promote greater access to political participation and decision-making. Youssouf stressed that African citizens must be involved in decisions affecting their communities. Turning to Africa's economic future, he described political parties as architects of the continent's future, emphasizing the need for institutions capable of shaping that future around the general public interest rather than partisan considerations. He emphasized the critical role of political parties in fostering democratic governance, peace, and development aligned with the African Union's Agenda 2063. Stressing the need for transparency in political financing, he called for strict regulations to combat corruption. Youssouf advocated for inclusive political participation, particularly for women and youth, and emphasized the importance of consensus on development priorities like education and infrastructure. He reaffirmed the AU's commitment to promoting democracy and stability across member states. (158 words)

ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, France Vow to Deepen Military and Strategic Cooperation - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia, France Vow to Deepen Military and Strategic Cooperation 6 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia and France have pledged to deepen their longstanding military and strategic cooperation, with renewed emphasis on military capacity building, knowledge transfer and regional peace and stability. The commitment was made during talks between Ethiopian Defense Minister Mohammed Idris and French Ambassador to Ethiopia Alexis Lamek in Addis Ababa on Wondsday. The meeting, part of the Defense Minister's ongoing military diplomacy engagements with foreign ambassadors, focused on strengthening the two countries' historical ties and expanding cooperation in military and strategic affairs. Minister Mohammed expressed appreciation for France's support in enhancing Ethiopia's military capabilities through knowledge transfer, strengthening institutional capacity and improving its preparedness for peacekeeping operations. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He also called on France to support Ethiopia's efforts to safeguard its legitimate and equitable interests in the region. On the ongoing Disarmament, Demobilization and Reintegration (DDR) process in the Tigray Region, the Minister urged France to extend the necessary support to ensure its successful implementation. Ambassador Lamek, for his part, reaffirmed France's commitment to strengthening its longstanding relations and multifaceted cooperation with Ethiopia. He underscored his country's readiness to enhance joint efforts in promoting regional peace and stability, while advancing military training and capacity-building cooperation. The renewed commitment signals both countries' interest in translating their longstanding diplomatic relations into stronger practical cooperation in defense, military development and regional security, as ENA learned. ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Urges African Political Parties to Prioritize Leadership Renewal, Long-Term Dev't 6 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed called on African political parties to embrace leadership renewal and build consensus on long-term national priorities. He also stressed that the continent's development must transcend electoral cycles and changes of government. The Prime Minister made the call while opening the Second African Political Parties Summit in Addis Ababa, where he proposed two key commitments for inclusion in the Addis Ababa Declaration: establishing consensus on long-term national development priorities and strengthening leadership development and succession across Africa. He emphasized that political parties should agree on strategic national goals with measurable milestones to ensure continuity of development efforts regardless of political transitions. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines PM Abiy elaborated that parties can maintain ideological and policy differences and compete for electoral support while working together on fundamental national interests and long-term development objectives. He also stressed that leadership succession is essential to sustaining development, warning that countries risk losing hard-won progress when incumbent leaders fail to prepare the next generation of leadership. Highlighting Ethiopia's experience in political inclusiveness, the Prime Minister said the country's reformed government has incorporated leaders from opposition political parties. This reflects an approach that values broader participation and shared responsibility, the Premier revealed. He noted that Ethiopia's Medemer philosophy encourages political actors to recognize and build on one another's contributions despite their differences, particularly when national interests call for collective action. Turning to economic transformation, PM Abiy outlined key measures undertaken through Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda, including opening the telecommunications, banking and competition sectors to foreign participation and introducing a market-based foreign exchange system. somalia.title: Mogadishu tourism: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees her city - BBC
somalia.content: Mogadishu tourism: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees her city Skip to content Watch Live British Broadcasting Corporation Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu 6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Fardowsa Hanshi BBC Somali Getty Images Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu. This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital. Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture. Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes. "It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old. The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara. But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers. Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea. Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity. "Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says. At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species. Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader wants visitors to experience the "beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu" Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia. He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago. "I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says. She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience. She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting. She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali. AFP via Getty Images A wide variety of fish are available in Mogadishu's markets Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu. The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow. However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security. Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down. But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation. Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital. Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life. About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department. Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city. But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive. AFP via Getty Images Lido beach is one of the most popular places for people to relax in Mogadishu "What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says. Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue. She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen. "I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says. Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden. Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade. Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking. American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice. His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media. "I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says. What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere. "It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says. Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC The sand dunes near Mogadishu remind some visitors of the Sahara Desert During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes. "The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says. Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage. "If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines." But visiting the country challenged those perceptions. "Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says. Mohamud Abdisamad/BBC Romanian Mihaela Patap says she prefers to visit new countries without preconceived ideas Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty. Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline. "The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says. Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness. "I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says. An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas. "I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says. She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia. "I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says. For Sucdi, that potential is personal. She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu. "Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says. "Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines." For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu. Football (CAF) has appointed match officials for the TotalEnergies AFCON 2027 Qualifier between Somalia and Ghana. The match will be played at the Essipong Sports Stadium on Monday, November 16, 2026, at 15:00 GMT . Namibian referee Mweshitsama Negongo Naftal will take charge of the game. He will be assisted by fellow Namibians Alex Muzibwane Lumponjani (Assistant I) and Klaus Masati Bonifatius (Assistant II), while Petrus Amutenya will serve as the Fourth Official. Sekamana Abdoul Khaliq from Rwanda will be the Match Commissioner, with Brian Nsubuga Miiro from Uganda appointed as the Referee Assessor. Danny Adotey from Ghana will be the Broadcast Venue Manager. Ghana will be aiming to bounce back in the qualifiers after two defeats in their opening matches against Côte d'Ivoire and The Gambia, with an eye on six points against Somalia to get their campaign back on track. somalia.summary: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has appointed Namibian officials for the upcoming AFCON 2027 Qualifier match between Somalia and Ghana, scheduled for November 16, 2026, at the Essipong Sports Stadium. The match will be officiated by referee Mweshitsama Negongo Naftal, supported by assistants Alex Muzibwane Lumponjani and Klaus Masati Bonifatius. Petrus Amutenya will serve as the Fourth Official, while Sekamana Abdoul Khaliq from Rwanda will act as the Match Commissioner, and Brian Nsubuga Miiro from Uganda will be the Referee Assessor. Ghana, having suffered two defeats in their initial qualifying matches against Côte d'Ivoire and The Gambia, is looking to secure a crucial victory against Somalia to revive their campaign and aim for six points in the qualifiers. The Ghana Football Association is focused on improving the team's performance in this critical match.

News Around the World Africa US forces leave important airfield in Somalia Troops exited Baledogle Airfield after 14 years, but will remain in the country, a military official told Task & Purpose. By Nicholas Slayton Published Nov 6, 2026 5:01 PM EST Add Task & Purpose (opens Google in a new window or tab) More information Adding us as a Preferred Source in Google by using this link indicates that you would like to see more of our content in Google News results. The U.S. military pulled all of its troops from a major air base in Somalia last month, after using the Baledogle Military Airfield for more than a decade as part of its counterterrorism mission in the country. Troops left the airfield, located only a few dozen miles from the capital of Mogadishu, but will remain in the country. Horn Observer first reported the exit, citing multiple people familiar with the base. A military official familiar with the matter confirmed to Task & Purpose that the troops left the base for other parts of Somalia. The official said that U.S. forces might return to Baledogle in the future. A spokesperson for U.S. Africa Command did not confirm reports of troops leaving, but said in a statement that the “U.S. military is an agile, mobile force. U.S. Africa Command repositions its forces to optimize for counterterror operations. In the interest of maintaining operational security, we do not discuss details of ongoing operations.” News Special operations guardians must ‘maneuver with their SOF counterparts,’ commander says By Patty Nieberg News Air Force sends F-16s to remote island in the western Aleutians By Nicholas Slayton News Drones built to look like birds evaded detection at Air Force tech exercise By Patty Nieberg It is not clear how many troops were assigned to the airfield before they were relocated, although the United States has kept dozens there in the past, supporting operations around the region. The airfield is roughly 60 miles southwest of Mogadishu and has been a focal point of the ongoing Somali civil war. In 2009, the militant group al-Shabaab captured Baledogle, using it as a training ground for its fighters for three years before African Union forces pushed them out. U.S. troops began operating at Baledogle in 2012, expanding their presence in the following years. Alongside counterterrorism missions, American troops trained Somali commandos. On Sept. 30, 2019, al-Shabaab forces attacked the airfield using a combination of vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices and small arms. American and Somali troops at the base engaged the militants for an hour, eventually driving them back. Despite some major shifts in U.S. operations on the African continent — including wrapping up combat missions against Islamic State militants in Nigeria and moving MQ-9 drones from Africa to Latin America — the military has continued its ongoing campaign against militants in Somalia. In October, American forces launched four separate airstrikes on al-Shabaab fighters in the country, per AFRICOM. Those are part of the expanded strike campaign since the start of the second Trump administration. Earlier this year the U.S. began a multi-million dollar upgrade project on an air base in Kenya that the American military uses for operations in the Horn of Africa. somalia.summary: U.S. forces have vacated Baledogle Airfield in Somalia after 14 years of operations, although they will continue their presence in the country. The airfield, located approximately 60 miles from Mogadishu, has been a strategic site for U.S. counterterrorism efforts, particularly against the militant group al-Shabaab. The exit was first reported by Horn Observer, and a military official confirmed that troops have relocated to other areas within Somalia, with the possibility of returning to Baledogle in the future. While the exact number of troops stationed at the airfield prior to their departure remains unclear, the U.S. military has historically maintained a significant presence there. The airfield has been pivotal in training Somali commandos and conducting operations against militants. Despite the withdrawal from Baledogle, U.S. forces have continued airstrikes against al-Shabaab, indicating an ongoing commitment to counterterrorism in the region.

somalia.content: Galmudug's New President Hands Over Personal Military Vehicle to Regional Security Ministry - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Security Galmudug Galmudug’s New President Hands Over Personal Military Vehicle to Regional Security Ministry November 6, 2026 4 min read DHUSAMAREB , Galmudug’s new President, Liibaan Ahmed Hassan, has formally handed over a military vehicle he personally owned and used during his election campaign to the Galmudug Ministry of Security, in a ceremony attended by federal President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. The handover, which took place during the inauguration events in Dhusamareb, marks one of Liibaan’s first public acts as president. The vehicle, described as a military-style vehicle, was used during the campaign that brought him to power and is now being transferred to the regional security apparatus. The ceremony was attended by President Mohamud, who had traveled to Dhusamareb for the inauguration, alongside federal and regional officials. The gesture is symbolically significant. It signals a transfer of personal resources to the state, and it comes at a time when Galmudug’s security forces are expected to assume greater responsibility for the region’s stability. The new president has pledged to prioritize security and intensify operations against Al-Shabaab , as FTL Somalia reported on his campaign promises . A Transition Under Federal Watch The handover ceremony is part of a broader inauguration process that has drawn federal and international attention. President Mohamud’s presence in Dhusamareb underscores the federal government’s investment in the transition. Liibaan was elected by the Galmudug House of Representatives on October 22, securing 72 of 89 votes, as FTL Somalia reported on the parliamentary vote . His victory consolidated the control of the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP), which had already won a dominant majority in the September 30 parliamentary rerun, as FTL Somalia reported on the JSP’s landslide . The path to Liibaan’s presidency was shaped by federal endorsement. President Mohamud endorsed him as the JSP’s sole candidate in May 2026, and outgoing President Qoor Qoor withdrew from the race in June after talks with federal officials, as FTL Somalia reported on his withdrawal . The federal government’s hand in the transition has been visible throughout, from the endorsement of Liibaan’s candidacy to the President’s attendance at the inauguration. The security context is urgent. Galmudug faces persistent threats from Al-Shabaab, clan disputes over land and resources, and the economic pressures of drought and displacement. The Somali National Army’s Land Forces commander, Brigadier General Sahal Abdullahi Omar, was in Dhusamareb for meetings with officers on operations against Al-Shabaab and troop readiness in the region, a sign that the federal military is actively engaged in Galmudug as the new leadership takes over. Critical Note The handover of a personal military vehicle to the Ministry of Security is a gesture that deserves acknowledgment. It is a small thing in material terms, but it signals a disposition. A president who transfers his own assets to the state is sending a message that the state’s institutions, not his personal network, are the proper repository of security resources. In a region where armed power has often been personal and clan-based, that message matters. But a vehicle is not a policy. Galmudug’s security challenges are structural: a long coastline, a porous border with Ethiopia, Al-Shabaab’s presence in rural areas, and a regional force that is still being built. Liibaan’s pledge to defeat Al-Shabaab within six months is ambitious to the point of being unrealistic. The handover of one vehicle does not change the balance of forces. It is a symbol, and symbols are useful, but they are not a substitute for the funding, training, and coordination that the Ministry of Security will need to do its job. The presence of President Mohamud at the ceremony is also a reminder of the federal government’s stake in Galmudug’s stability. The federal government has invested political capital in Liibaan’s presidency, endorsing his candidacy and attending his inauguration. That investment creates an obligation. If Galmudug’s security deteriorates, the federal government will share the blame. If it improves, the federal government will share the credit. The handover of a vehicle is a small down payment on a much larger commitment that the federal government and the new regional administration have both made. This act symbolizes a commitment to state resources over personal power, particularly in a region facing security challenges from Al-Shabaab and clan disputes. somalia.summary: Uganda has initiated the withdrawal of its troops from Somalia, marking a significant shift in its foreign security commitment. The Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) has been stationed in Somalia since March 2007, becoming the first foreign military to intervene in the country, which was then plagued by clan warfare. Currently, approximately 4,500 troops are part of the African Union (AU) mission in Somalia, supplemented by around 2,000 additional troops through bilateral agreements. The withdrawal raises questions about the future security landscape in Somalia, particularly regarding the stability and effectiveness of local forces in the absence of UPDF support. As Uganda begins this exit, the implications for Somalia's ongoing conflict and the broader regional security dynamics remain uncertain, prompting discussions on the next steps for both Somalia and the international community involved in peacekeeping efforts.

somalia.title: Somalia’s WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Somalia's WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Economy & Business Nationwide Somalia’s WTO Bid Nears Completion After Technical Mission in Mogadishu November 6, 2026 6 min read MOGADISHU , Somalia’s decade-long bid to join the World Trade Organization has moved closer to completion after a week-long technical mission in Mogadishu brought most of its accession documents close to final, ahead of a working party meeting expected in 2027. A team led by the WTO’s Head of Accessions Division, working alongside experts from the International Trade Centre at the Somali government’s request, spent October 10 to 15 reviewing the documents behind Somalia’s bid. The mission, funded by the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office through the ITC’s Making Trade Happen project, refined Somalia’s replies to WTO members’ questions on customs, import licensing, animal and plant health, technical standards, and intellectual property, and mapped the laws still needed for compliance . The teams also prepared Somalia’s first offers to open its markets for goods and services. A joint session with the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area examined how Somalia’s regional commitments and its WTO bid can reinforce each other. Somalia joined the EAC in 2024, and the bloc’s common external tariff will shape its offer on goods . “The UK is proud to support Somalia’s ambition to join the World Trade Organization through our partnership with the International Trade Centre. Bringing WTO expertise to Mogadishu for the first time is helping turn that ambition into practical progress,” said British Ambassador to Somalia Charles King . “Ultimately, this is about creating opportunities for businesses, attracting investment and creating jobs for Somalis.” The Economic Case Somalia applied to join the WTO in 2015, and its working party first met in Geneva in February 2025. Somali leaders have framed accession as a route to growth and investment, arguing that binding international rules on trade would reduce the uncertainty that deters foreign investors and open markets for Somali products . The economic logic is straightforward, though the starting point is difficult. Somalia has about 18 million people and the longest coastline on the African mainland, but its exports remain concentrated in livestock. Live animal sales earned $576 million in 2025, mostly in the Gulf, according to ITC Trade Map, more than double the export earnings from seven years ago . As FTL Somalia reported on the concentration of Somalia’s export base , livestock still accounts for roughly 75 percent of exports, leaving the economy vulnerable to import bans and price shocks in a single sector. WTO membership could help address that vulnerability. The organization’s rules on animal health and food safety provide a framework that importing countries recognize, potentially clearing a path for Somali livestock exports to markets that currently restrict them. But the path is not automatic. Somalia would need to demonstrate that its veterinary controls, inspection systems, and certification procedures meet international standards, and it would need to maintain those standards consistently. The broader trade picture is also challenging. As FTL Somalia reported on Somalia’s trade gap , imports continue to far outstrip exports, creating a structural deficit that WTO membership alone cannot resolve. Joining the organization would lower barriers to Somali goods in foreign markets, but it would also require Somalia to lower its own barriers, exposing domestic producers to competition they may not be ready to face. Regional Integration and the WTO Track Somalia’s WTO bid is not proceeding in isolation. The country joined the EAC in 2024 and formally acceded to the African Continental Free Trade Area as its 50th member, opening access to a market of 1.4 billion consumers, as FTL Somalia reported on the AfCFTA accession . The two tracks are complementary in principle. The EAC’s common external tariff will shape Somalia’s WTO offer on goods, and the AfCFTA provides a framework for expanding intra-African trade that the WTO’s global rules do not directly address. But they also create complexity. Somalia’s negotiators must ensure that its commitments to the EAC and the AfCFTA are consistent with its WTO obligations, and that the preferences it grants to regional partners do not violate the WTO’s most-favored-nation principle. The government has framed regional integration as a means of creating opportunities for Somali traders, as FTL Somalia reported on the minister’s remarks about EAC membership . The WTO accession process adds a global dimension to that strategy, but it also imposes disciplines that the government will need to implement across customs, standards, and regulatory agencies that are still being built. Critical Note The WTO mission to Mogadishu is a genuine step forward. The fact that WTO and ITC experts spent a week working alongside Somali officials, refining documents and preparing market access offers, is evidence that the accession process has moved beyond rhetoric into technical work. The UK’s funding and the ITC’s expertise have made that work possible. But the completion of accession documents is not the same as accession. Somalia still needs to finalize its offers, answer remaining questions from WTO members, enact the laws it has mapped, and demonstrate that it can implement the commitments it makes. The working party meeting expected in 2027 is a milestone, not a finish line. Accession negotiations can take years, and the terms Somalia accepts will determine whether membership delivers the benefits its leaders promise. The economic case is real but conditional. WTO rules can help Somali livestock reach new markets, but only if Somalia can meet the health and safety standards those rules require. Membership can attract investment, but only if the legal and regulatory environment is stable enough to reassure investors. And it can support regional integration, but only if Somalia’s commitments to the EAC, the AfCFTA, and the WTO are coherent and consistently implemented. The government has spent a decade pursuing WTO membership. The technical mission in October brought that goal closer. The harder work, of building the institutions and implementing the rules that membership requires, is still ahead. The documents are nearly final. The capacity to honor them is not. somalia.summary: Somalia's bid to join the World Trade Organization (WTO) is progressing, nearing completion following a technical mission in Mogadishu from October 10 to 15. Led by the WTO's Head of Accessions Division, the mission focused on refining Somalia's accession documents and preparing market access offers. This effort, funded by the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, aims to address questions regarding customs, licensing, and health standards. Somalia's leaders view WTO membership as a pathway to economic growth and investment, particularly for its livestock sector, which constitutes 75% of exports. However, challenges remain, including the need to meet international standards and manage commitments to regional trade agreements like the East African Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area. While the technical mission marks significant progress, Somalia must still finalize its offers and demonstrate its capacity to implement WTO rules effectively before full accession can be achieved. The next working party meeting is anticipated in 2027. (158 words)

football.content: الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج دول الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ من مباراة الهلال ضد رايون سبورت الرواندي (Facebook/alhilalsc.official) 5 نوفمبر 2026 الهلال يتعثر.. ما المكاسب أمام رايون سبورت رغم إهدار الفوز؟ الهلال السوداني الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أحبط الهلال جماهيره وانقاد للتعادل بنتيجة 1-1 أمام نظيره رايون سبورت الرواندي، اليوم الأربعاء 4 نوفمبر، على ملعب "كيغالي بيليه" ضمن الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي، الذي يشهد مشاركة الهلال ومواطنه المريخ . وفرط "الموج الأزرق" في فرصة تحقيق الفوز، مكتفيا بالتعادل بعد أن بادر بالتسجيل عبر قائده وهدافه محمد عبد الرحمن، قبل أن يدرك المنافس التعادل في الرمق الأخير من المباراة، ليهدر الفريق فرصة مثالية لتقليص الفارق مع صدارة الدوري، في انتظار خوض مبارياته المؤجلة الثلاث. مكاسب مضاعفة لـ"غربال" رغم تفريط الهلال في الفوز باستقباله هدف التعادل في اللحظات الأخيرة، إلا أن "الكابيتانو" محمد عبد الرحمن نجح في وضع فريقه بالمقدمة بهدف رائع، محققا مكاسب شخصية بتعزيز سجله التهديفي وتأكيد عودته القوية قبل المواجهات المرتقبة في مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا عقب فترة التوقف الدولي. كما سيمنح مدرب المنتخب "كواسي أبياه" خياراً هجومياً مميزاً لاستعادة فاعلية "صقور الجديان" التهديفية، بخوضه مباراتين حاسمتين أمام المنتخب السنغالي بتصفيات بطولة الأمم الأفريقية. اقرأ أيضًا مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري وسيحظى مدرب النادي الأزرق بفرصة مثالية لتجهيز عناصره عبر خوض تجارب ودية قوية خلال فترة التوقف الدولي، إذ سيلتحق 16 من أبرز نجومه بمنتخباتهم الوطنية، منهم 13 لاعبا في صفوف "صقور الجديان", و3 آخرون مع منتخبات بلدانهم. وسيعمل المدرب خلال هذا الغياب على إعداد البدائل، سعيا لتحقيق أفضل النتائج في دور المجموعات بدوري أبطال أفريقيا. وقرر المدرب جوزيف زينباور استغلال فترة التوقف بإجراء مباريات إعدادية، على أن يخوض الفريق مواجهة واحدة في الدوري الرواندي عقب التوقف، ليبدأ بعدها رحلة شاقة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بملاقاة حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر الجاري، ثم يحل ضيفا على المغرب الفاسي في 5 ديسمبر المقبل، قبل أن يختتم هذه المرحلة الأولى بصدام قوي أمام بيراميدز المصري. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق football.summary: تعادل فريق الهلال السوداني مع رايون سبورت الرواندي بنتيجة 1-1 في مباراة أقيمت يوم 4 نوفمبر 2026، ضمن الجولة السابعة من الدوري الرواندي. رغم البداية القوية بتسجيل قائد الفريق محمد عبد الرحمن هدف التقدم، إلا أن الهلال أهدر فرصة الفوز بعد أن أدرك المنافس التعادل في اللحظات الأخيرة. هذا التعادل أحبط جماهير الهلال، لكنه يحمل بعض المكاسب، حيث عزز عبد الرحمن سجله التهديفي، مما يعزز فرصه في المباريات المقبلة، خاصة في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. المدرب جوزيف زينباور يخطط لاستغلال فترة التوقف الدولي لإجراء مباريات ودية، حيث سيلتحق 16 لاعباً من الهلال بمنتخباتهم الوطنية. بعد فترة التوقف، سيواجه الهلال حوريا كوناكري الغيني في 28 نوفمبر، ثم المغرب الفاسي وبيراميدز المصري، مما يتطلب تجهيز الفريق بشكل جيد لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية.

football.title: مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا - winwin
football.content: مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا مدرب الهلال السوداني يكشف أزمة قاتلة قبل دوري أبطال أفريقيا مباريات اليوم رياضات كرة القدم الأخبار فيديو البطولات البرامج أبطال أفريقيا الهلال السوداني مصطفى كرشوم الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' وصف الألماني جوزيف زينباور مدرب الهلال السوداني، نتيجة التعادل (1-1) التي حققها فريقه أمام رايون سبورت الرواندي في الجولة السابعة من مسابقة الدوري الرواندي بالسيئة، مؤكدا أن فريقه فرط في فوز كان في المتناول بعد تقدمه المبكر، قبل التعهد بمعالجة السلبيات التي رافقت أداء الفريق في المباريات الأخيرة. وأوضح المدرب عبر مقطع فيديو نشره الموقع الرسمي للنادي، أنه لم يحظ بفرصة كافية لخوض تجارب ودية قبل انطلاقة الموسم للوقوف على إمكانات جميع اللاعبين، خاصة مع انضمام عناصر جديدة خلال فترة الانتقالات الصيفية، مشيرًا إلى أن فترة التوقف الدولي ستساعده في تجهيز الفريق بشكل أفضل. مدرب الهلال يشيد بنجميه كما أشاد زينباور بنجميه سفيان فريد و مصطفى كرشوم ، قائلا: "قدم الحارس سفيان مباراة متميزة، ويعد كرشوم مدافعا رائعا يمتاز بالهدوء والقدرة الفائقة على استخلاص الكرة وبناء اللعب". وأضاف: "تقدمنا مبكرا ولم نستثمر الفرص التي أتيحت لنا، واستقبلنا هدفا في الرمق الأخير من المباراة؛ كان يتعين علينا تسجيل هدفين على الأقل لنحسم المباراة، ولكننا لم نستثمر الفرص، علينا إيجاد حلول لاستقبال الأهداف المتأخرة، وبالمجمل، لست راضيا عن هذه النتيجة". اقرأ أيضًا رامي كمال: الهلال يستحق تكريمًا سياديًا وسنتوج باللقب القاري المريخ يربك تحضيرات الهلال لمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا كما كشف زينباور عن أسباب تذبذب الأداء والتغييرات المستمرة في تشكيل فريقه مؤخرًا، قائلا: "لقد أضفنا عناصر جديدة خلال فترة الانتقالات، لدينا لاعبون شباب نرغب في منحهم فرصة المشاركة؛ لذا نجري هذه التعديلات لنقف على مستوياتهم، ونأمل أن يقدموا الإضافة المرجوة". وأضاف: "واجهنا منافسين أقوياء، على غرار فريق رايون الذي تميز باللياقة العالية والقوة البدنية، وسنواجه تحديات صعبة تستدعي وفرة في العناصر". وختم المدرب الألماني حديثه قائلاً: "نسعى لمزيد من التطور، ويتعين علينا مواصلة العمل الجاد لاستثمار الفرص في تطوير الجوانب البدنية والتكتيكية قبل المباريات الصعبة التي تنتظرنا في دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، إذ يجب أن نستعد جيدا لنبلغ مرحلة متميزة من الجاهزية حتى نتمكن من مجابهة التحديات المرتقبة". النشرة البريدية اشترك
